answer:
Aleatoric uncertainty is conditional outcome variability under the observed features; epistemic uncertainty concerns the fitted model or unknown parameters. With $\theta$ distributed according to model uncertainty, total variance decomposes as $\operatorname{Var}(Y|x,D)=\mathbb E_\theta\operatorname{Var}(Y|x,\theta)+\operatorname{Var}_\theta\mathbb E(Y|x,\theta)$. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book2.html)

More representative data can reduce the second term. The first may remain even with infinite data under the same features, though better sensors/features can reduce it; thus the distinction is relative to the information and model available. A noisy thermometer illustrates measurement variability, while an unfamiliar climate illustrates lack of knowledge. Estimate both with calibrated models and check shift: a neat decomposition inside a misspecified model does not guarantee correct real-world uncertainty.
